content: Introduction Individuals living with HIV often experience various coinfections, comorbidities, and other concurrent health conditions. These factors significantly influence their treatment and care, including the timing and selection of antiretroviral (ARV) drugs. This section provides a concise overview of the most common and clinically significant conditions affecting people with HIV. It highlights key recommendations from existing WHO guidelines and related materials, focusing on screening, prophylaxis, and the timing of antiretroviral therapy (ART) initiation for these conditions. However, it does not delve into detailed management strategies. References to relevant, previously published recommendations are provided. It is important to note that these recommendations were not reviewed during the 2015 guideline development process. Evidence reviews conducted in 2015 addressed presumptive treatment for tuberculosis (TB), depression, and cardiovascular disease in people living with HIV. While no formal recommendation was made for presumptive TB treatment, guidance is provided. New recommendations are included for the screening and management of cardiovascular disease and depression in individuals with HIV. Co-trimoxazole Prophylaxis: Background and Rationale Co-trimoxazole (CTX) is a fixed-dose combination of two antimicrobial agents, sulfamethoxazole and trimethoprim, used to treat a range of bacterial, fungal, and protozoan infections. CTX prophylaxis is a practical, well-tolerated, and cost-effective intervention to reduce HIV-related morbidity and mortality. It is an off-patent drug widely available in resource-limited settings. The first WHO guidelines on CTX prophylaxis in resource-limited settings, published in 2006, recommended its use as an integral component of HIV care. These guidelines were reviewed in 2014 and updated in the context of expanded access to and earlier initiation of ART. Recent evidence has demonstrated that with broader access to ART, CTX prophylaxis provides additional benefits beyond preventing certain AIDS-associated opportunistic infections, such as Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PCP) and toxoplasmosis. These benefits include reduced HIV-related mortality in individuals with low CD4 cell counts and prevention of malaria and severe bacterial infections (SBIs) in both adults and children with HIV. Recommendations for Co-trimoxazole Prophylaxis in Adults CTX prophylaxis is recommended for adults, including pregnant women, with severe or advanced HIV clinical disease (WHO stage 3 or 4) and/or a CD4 count ≤ 350 cells/mm³. In settings with high prevalence of malaria and/or severe bacterial infections, CTX prophylaxis should be initiated regardless of CD4 cell count or WHO stage. Discontinuation of CTX prophylaxis may be considered in adults who are clinically stable on ART, with evidence of immune recovery and viral suppression. However, in settings with high prevalence of malaria and/or severe bacterial infections, CTX prophylaxis should be continued regardless of CD4 cell count or WHO clinical stage. Routine CTX prophylaxis should also be provided to all HIV-infected patients with active TB disease, regardless of CD4 cell count. Recommendations for Co-trimoxazole Prophylaxis in Infants, Children, and Adolescents CTX prophylaxis is recommended for all infants, children, and adolescents with HIV, irrespective of clinical or immune status. Priority should be given to children under five years of age, regardless of CD4 cell count or clinical stage, and to children with severe or advanced HIV clinical disease (WHO stage 3 or 4) and/or a CD4 count ≤ 350 cells/mm³. In settings with high prevalence of malaria and/or severe bacterial infections, CTX prophylaxis should be continued until adulthood, regardless of ART status. In settings with low prevalence of malaria and bacterial infections, CTX prophylaxis may be discontinued for children aged five years and older who are clinically stable and virally suppressed on ART for at least six months, with a CD4 count > 350 cells/mm³. CTX prophylaxis is also recommended for HIV-exposed infants starting at 4–6 weeks of age and should be continued until HIV infection is excluded through appropriate testing after cessation of breastfeeding. Effectiveness of Co-trimoxazole Prophylaxis The effectiveness of CTX prophylaxis in reducing mortality among individuals starting ART with a CD4 count ≤ 350 cells/mm³ and/or WHO stage 3 or 4 disease is supported by moderate-quality evidence from observational studies. A systematic review has shown that CTX prophylaxis reduces mortality, severe bacterial infections, malaria, and hospitalizations in adults and adolescents with HIV, regardless of clinical or immunological parameters. Randomized clinical trials in children with HIV have demonstrated survival benefits of CTX prophylaxis, irrespective of age or CD4 count, particularly in settings with high prevalence of malaria and/or severe bacterial infections. Continuation of CTX prophylaxis in such settings, regardless of ART status, age, CD4 count, or WHO clinical stage, is recommended based on data showing significant reductions in hospitalization, malaria, and diarrhea. Implementation Considerations for Co-trimoxazole Prophylaxis Key barriers to implementing CTX prophylaxis include supply chain issues leading to stock-outs, costs imposed on patients for medication or monitoring, inadequate training and supervision of healthcare workers, low coverage of HIV testing and counseling, and lack of coordination across programs. To address these challenges, countries should adapt WHO guidelines to their national context, strengthen drug supply management systems, secure financing to eliminate patient costs, and coordinate with malaria programs. Training and sensitization of healthcare workers, community-level education, and monitoring of adherence to policies and the impact of CTX prophylaxis on population health are also critical. High-quality CTX formulations should be provided, and toxicity monitoring should be conducted, particularly for chronic use. Tuberculosis and HIV Tuberculosis (TB) is the leading cause of death among hospitalized adults and children with HIV, accounting for approximately one-third of all mortality. Autopsy studies have shown a pooled prevalence of nearly 40% for TB in individuals with HIV, with many cases previously undiagnosed. Routine TB symptom screening using an algorithm that includes fever, cough, weight loss, and night sweats can help identify individuals who require expedited TB diagnosis or preventive therapy. The combined use of isoniazid preventive therapy (IPT) and ART has demonstrated both TB prevention and mortality benefits, even in individuals with higher CD4 counts. Timely initiation of ART and implementation of the Three I’s for HIV/TB (intensified TB case-finding, IPT, and infection control) are critical to reducing TB-related mortality in people with HIV. Improving Implementation of Co-trimoxazole Prophylaxis To enhance the implementation of CTX prophylaxis policies, countries should adapt WHO guidelines to their specific contexts, ensure sustained availability of CTX at healthcare facilities, and eliminate patient costs for the medication. Coordination with malaria programs is essential, particularly regarding recommendations for intermittent preventive treatment of malaria in pregnancy and seasonal malaria chemoprophylaxis in children under five years. Training and sensitization of healthcare workers, community education, and monitoring of adherence to policies are necessary to improve coverage and impact. High-quality CTX formulations should be provided, and adverse reactions should be monitored, especially in the context of chronic use.
